headline: Genetic Test Could Unlock Aspirin's Dementia-Fighting Power
meta_description: Researchers find low-dose aspirin cuts dementia risk by 70% in people with specific genetics, offering hope for personalized prevention.
summary_short: A Monash University study reveals that people with certain genetic profiles taking low-dose aspirin had 70% lower dementia risk—but safety concerns remain.
body:
A new analysis from Monash University has uncovered an unexpected twist in dementia prevention: low-dose aspirin may dramatically reduce risk for older adults with a particular genetic profile, even though previous studies found no overall protective effect across all populations. Among people in the highest 20 percent of platelet count genetic scores, just 1 percent of aspirin users developed dementia compared with 3.3 percent taking a placebo—a 70 percent lower relative risk. Published in Alzheimer's & Dementia: The Journal of the Alzheimer's Association, the findings involved genetic data from more than 13,500 participants in the landmark ASPREE Trial, suggesting that a person's genetic makeup could eventually guide which prevention strategies work best.

The discovery opens a door to personalized medicine, particularly as dementia becomes increasingly common. Dementia Australia estimates approximately 446,500 people in Australia are living with the condition in 2026, a number expected to exceed one million by 2065. What makes this finding remarkable is that the genetic signal researchers identified involves platelet biology—not the well-established genetic risk factors typically linked to Alzheimer's disease. This points toward a new avenue for investigation that scientists hadn't previously emphasized.

However, the promise comes with caution. The same genetic group saw major bleeding occur in 4.4 percent of aspirin users compared with 2.1 percent receiving a placebo. Researchers emphasize the results must be confirmed in other populations and through trials specifically designed for people with this genetic profile before any medical recommendations can be made. "People shouldn't start taking aspirin to prevent dementia on the basis of this study without consulting with their doctor," the research team stated. If the findings hold up, the fact that aspirin is already cheap and widely available could make personalized dementia prevention genuinely accessible.
quick_facts: Monash University study of 13,500+ ASPREE Trial participants
70% lower relative dementia risk for people with specific platelet genetics
1% of aspirin users vs. 3.3% of placebo users developed dementia
Australia: 446,500 people with dementia in 2026, projected over 1 million by 2065
Higher bleeding risk: 4.4% aspirin users vs. 2.1% placebo users
